# 10 — Limitations & Future Work

*What this system can't do, and what to build next. Ordered by value, not by ease.*

---

## 10.1 Limitations, stated plainly

### L1 — The dataset is synthetic

**The big one.** Every number in this repository comes from URLs generated by `src/dataset.py`. The generator reproduces eight documented attack patterns and includes deliberate hard cases, but it cannot reproduce the full messiness of the real web. Expect roughly 93–96% on a real corpus, not 99.25%.

### L2 — Compromised legitimate domains are near-invisible

`https://realbakery.com/wp-content/uploads/paypal/login.php` — the domain is genuine, so every hostname feature says "safe". Only `brand_outside_domain` fires, from the path. Change the path to `/x/a.php` and nothing fires at all. This is a limit of the *approach*, not the implementation.

### L3 — No temporal information

Domain age is one of the strongest real-world phishing signals: a domain registered three days ago hosting a bank login page is almost certainly malicious. Getting it requires a WHOIS lookup, which is a network request — ruled out by the latency and safety constraints in [doc 01](01-problem-statement.md).

### L4 — Hand-maintained lists go stale

`SUSPICIOUS_TLDS`, `SHORTENERS`, `BRANDS`, `SENSITIVE_WORDS` are all hand-written. Attackers move to new TLDs; new brands become targets. Without quarterly review, accuracy decays quietly — which is worse than failing loudly.

### L5 — The domain parser is wrong for multi-part suffixes

Last-two-labels reads `www.bbc.co.uk`'s registered domain as `co.uk`. Affects ~8% of domains, consistently across both classes so it doesn't bias the classifier, but it's incorrect.

### L6 — The explanations aren't the model's reasoning

`explain()` is a hand-written rule layer that happens to track the model's learned importances. A 200-tree ensemble's actual decision path isn't expressible in five bullets. The docstring says this; presenting it otherwise would be dishonest.

### L7 — Not production-grade

Flask dev server, no rate limiting, no model versioning, no drift monitoring, no retraining schedule.

### L8 — English-only

`SENSITIVE_WORDS` are English. Phishing targeting Hindi, Spanish or Mandarin speakers uses different vocabulary and would slip through.

---

## 10.2 What to build next

### Tier 1 — Highest value

#### 1. Evaluate on real data

**The single biggest credibility gain available.** Everything else is secondary to this.

```bash
# 1. Get a PhishTank API key, download verified phishing URLs
# 2. Download the Tranco top-1M list
# 3. Append realistic paths to the Tranco domains  (critical — see below)
# 4. Write both to data/urls.csv as url,label
# 5. python -m src.train
```

No code changes. `src/train.py` uses `data/urls.csv` if it exists.

**The trap:** if every legitimate URL is a bare domain (`https://google.com`) and every phishing URL has a path, the model learns "has a path → phishing" and reports 99% while being useless. Append realistic paths to the legitimate domains.

*Effort: 1–2 days. Impact: turns "an interesting prototype" into "a defensible result".*

#### 2. Add a domain-reputation feature

This fixes two of the three false positives in [doc 08 §8.3](08-results-and-evaluation.md#83-every-url-the-model-got-wrong) directly.

```python
TOP_DOMAINS = load_tranco_top_100k()      # a set, ~1 MB

"domain_in_top_100k":  int(registered_domain in TOP_DOMAINS),
"domain_rank_bucket":  bucket_of(TOP_DOMAINS.get(registered_domain, 999_999)),
```

`stackoverflow.com` gets flagged at 0.948 because the model learned "HTTPS + bare domain" from a generator imbalance. A single feature saying "`stackoverflow.com` is a top-100 domain" overrides that immediately, and would also fix the `icicibank.com` false positive. Still fully offline — the list ships as a file.

*Effort: half a day. Impact: likely the largest single accuracy gain of anything here.*

#### 3. Correct the suffix parsing

```bash
pip install tldextract
```

```python
import tldextract
def _registered_domain(hostname):
    parts = tldextract.extract(hostname)
    return f"{parts.domain}.{parts.suffix}", parts.suffix
```

One function body. Do it before running on real data, where multi-part suffixes are common.

*Effort: 30 minutes.*

---

### Tier 2 — Meaningful improvements

#### 4. SHAP for real explanations

```python
import shap
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model.named_steps["clf"])
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(scaled_row)
```

Replaces the rule-based `explain()` with true per-prediction attributions: *this* URL was flagged because `num_sensitive_words=4` contributed +0.31 and `suspicious_tld=1` contributed +0.22. Honest, and it renders beautifully as a waterfall chart in the web UI.

*Effort: 1 day.*

#### 5. Tune the decision threshold properly

Plot precision and recall against threshold from 0.05 to 0.95, pick the point matching your tolerance. For a security tool, recall should be weighted higher — the right threshold is probably 0.35–0.40, not 0.5. Report F2 alongside F1.

*Effort: half a day.*

#### 6. Compare against character n-gram TF-IDF

The main alternative to hand-crafted features. Character 3–5-grams + TF-IDF + linear SVM. Even if it wins on accuracy, the comparison is valuable: it quantifies what hand-crafted features buy you in explainability, and a hybrid (28 features + top-N n-grams) may beat both.

*Effort: 1 day.*

#### 7. Handle class imbalance

Real phishing is a tiny fraction of all URLs. Add `class_weight="balanced"`, report precision-recall AUC instead of ROC-AUC (PR-AUC is the honest metric under heavy imbalance), and consider SMOTE for the minority class.

*Effort: half a day, but required for any real deployment.*

---

### Tier 3 — Bigger projects

#### 8. Browser extension

Detection that never reaches a user helps nobody. A Manifest V3 extension that checks links on hover and warns before navigation:

```
[content script] intercept link hover/click
        │
        ▼
[background worker] POST /api/check
        │
        ▼
[warning overlay] if P(phishing) > threshold
```

The API already exists. The work is the extension plus a hosted backend — or, better, port `features.py` to JavaScript and run a small model entirely client-side, so no URLs leave the browser. That privacy property matters: users are pasting links they may not want to send anywhere.

*Effort: 1–2 weeks.*

#### 9. Multilingual support

Translate `SENSITIVE_WORDS` into Hindi, Spanish, Mandarin, Portuguese, Arabic. Add transliteration handling (`verificar`, `सत्यापित`). Needed for any non-English-speaking user base.

*Effort: 1 week plus native-speaker review.*

#### 10. Deep learning comparison

A character-level CNN or a small transformer over the raw URL string learns its own features. Published work (URLNet, and BERT-family models fine-tuned on URLs) reports strong results. Worth running as a comparison — but note the trade-off: a neural model is harder to explain, slower at inference, and needs far more data. If it only matches 28 hand-crafted features, the simpler system wins.

*Effort: 1–2 weeks, GPU helpful.*

#### 11. Production hardening

| Item | What |
|---|---|
| Serving | Gunicorn + nginx, or FastAPI + uvicorn |
| Containers | Dockerfile + docker-compose |
| Rate limiting | Flask-Limiter, per-IP |
| Caching | LRU on recently-seen URLs |
| Versioning | Timestamp + metrics in the model file; support rollback |
| Monitoring | Track prediction distribution — a sudden shift means concept drift |
| Retraining | Weekly scheduled job on fresh PhishTank data |
| CI | GitHub Actions: run tests, train, fail the build if F1 drops |

*Effort: 2–3 weeks.*

---

## 10.3 Suggested order

```
Week 1   Real data evaluation  +  tldextract fix
         └── you now have defensible numbers

Week 2   Domain reputation feature  +  threshold tuning
         └── the largest accuracy gains, cheaply

Week 3   SHAP explanations  +  n-gram comparison
         └── depth for a report or paper

Week 4+  Browser extension  or  production hardening
         └── depending on whether the goal is a product or a paper
```

Weeks 1 and 2 turn this from a working prototype into a result worth publishing. Everything after is scope.

---

## 10.4 If you extend this

Three things to preserve, because they are what make the project defensible:

1. **Keep the hard cases.** The moment the dataset gets easy, every model scores 100% and the evaluation stops meaning anything.
2. **Keep stating the synthetic-data caveat.** A qualified 99.25% is more credible than an unqualified one.
3. **Keep the error analysis.** [Doc 08 §8.3](08-results-and-evaluation.md#83-every-url-the-model-got-wrong) — naming all nine URLs the model got wrong and explaining exactly why — is worth more than any headline metric. It is what surfaced the bare-domain artifact that the 99.25% headline hid completely.
